title: How to embed images in email
author: Stefan Bogdanescu

content:
# The MIME Boundary: Embedding Images Without Third-Party Tools Embedding an image in an email is fundamentally different from linking to one on a web page. When you place an `` tag pointing to `https://example.com/logo.png`, the recipient's email client attempts to fetch that resource over HTTP or HTTPS. This approach fails in many contexts: corporate firewalls block external connections, mobile data plans throttle background image loading, and strict privacy settings disable remote content by default. To guarantee the image appears inline with your text, you must use a Data URI or, more commonly for production, a MIME multipart embedding strategy. The core mechanism relies on how email clients parse the message body. A simple text email uses the `text/plain` format. An HTML email requires `text/html`. However, neither can contain binary image data directly. The solution is to wrap the entire message in a `multipart/mixed` structure. This container allows you to include both the HTML content and the raw image bytes as separate parts within the same transmission envelope. To achieve this without third-party libraries, you must understand the role of MIME boundaries. A boundary string (e.g., `----WebKitFormBoundary7MA4YWxkTrZu0gW`) acts as a delimiter separating the different parts of the email. The client generating the email sets the `Content-Type` header for the root message to `multipart/mixed; boundary="..."`. Inside this wrapper, you define a part for the HTML body with `Content-Type: text/html`, and another part for the image with `Content-Type: image/png` (or JPEG/GIF). Crucially, the image part must not be referenced by a URL. Instead, the HTML `` tag must point to the specific Content-ID (CID) header assigned to that image part. When constructing this manually in PHP, you are essentially building a multipart stream. You start with an empty string and append each section prefixed by the boundary line (`--boundary\r\n`). The first section contains your HTML. Inside that HTML, the `src` attribute of your `` tag looks like `cid:unique-id`. The second section contains the binary image data, followed by a closing boundary (`--boundary--\r\n`). Here is a conceptual representation of how the headers and body structure must look: ```text Content-Type: multipart/mixed; boundary="----=_Part_123456.789012" ------=_Part_123456.789012 Content-Type: text/html; charset="UTF-8"

Please see our logo below:

------=_Part_123456.789012 Content-Type: image/png Content-ID: ... ------=_Part_123456.789012-- ``` The `Content-ID` header in the MIME part must match the value inside the `cid:` scheme of the HTML tag exactly, including the domain part if present. This identity link is what allows modern email clients to render the image inline rather than prompting the user to download it. There are significant trade-offs to consider when rolling your own multipart email generation. The most critical pitfall lies in handling binary data. If you use standard string concatenation or file operations without properly encoding the image bytes, you risk corrupting the MIME stream. In PHP, this often means using `fopen` with the binary mode flag or ensuring that no newline characters are accidentally introduced into the image payload unless they are part of the actual file format. Another consideration is the sheer size of the email. Embedding images directly inflates the message size because you are transmitting the full binary data every time the email is sent, regardless of whether the recipient has seen it before. This contrasts with linking to a hosted asset, which allows for caching and CDN optimization. However, for transactional emails like receipts or welcome sequences where brand consistency is paramount and image loading reliability is non-negotiable, embedding remains the industry standard. If you are working within the Laravel ecosystem, while manual construction is possible, leveraging existing packages often simplifies boundary management and header handling. The `laravelcompany.com` platform offers specific resources on managing complex email structures if your project outgrows the need for manual MIME stream manipulation. Understanding the underlying MIME structure, however, ensures that you can debug issues when those tools behave unexpectedly or when you are constrained by strict security policies that forbid external libraries.
